articles.title: Vector databases and similarity search
articles.concept: A vector index finds nearby embeddings under a chosen similarity metric. Approximate nearest-neighbor search trades some exact recall for speed and memory efficiency.
articles.mechanism: Normalize vectors when the embedding model and metric require it, version the encoder, and store dimensions explicitly. Tune approximate-search parameters against an exact-search baseline. Apply authorization and metadata filters without silently reducing relevant candidates below the required recall, and measure results on real query distributions.
articles.boundary: Embeddings from different model versions are generally incompatible. Similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities of correctness.
articles.example: An index migration builds a second collection and compares retrieval before switching traffic.
articles.application: Large semantic search services with predictable retrieval quality.

articles.title: Hybrid retrieval and reranking
articles.concept: Hybrid search combines lexical and semantic retrieval. A reranker then scores a smaller candidate set with more expensive query-document interaction.
articles.mechanism: Run keyword and vector retrieval under the same authorization constraints. Deduplicate by stable passage ID, fuse rankings using a documented rule, and rerank a bounded candidate pool. Evaluate candidate recall before reranking and final evidence precision afterward so improvements are attributable to the correct stage.
articles.boundary: Raw scores from different retrievers are not necessarily comparable. Reranking cannot recover a relevant passage absent from the candidate pool.
articles.example: A product support search uses lexical matching for exact error codes and embeddings for paraphrased symptoms.
articles.application: Technical support and enterprise search containing identifiers and natural language.

articles.title: Advanced RAG and retrieval evaluation
articles.concept: Advanced RAG adds selective query rewriting, decomposition, or iterative retrieval when a single lookup cannot supply sufficient evidence. Extra steps must justify their complexity.
articles.mechanism: Define answerable tasks and annotate the evidence needed for each. Measure recall over required evidence units, not merely whether any relevant passage appeared. Compare fixed pipelines with bounded iterative retrieval using the same corpus and budgets. Trace each retrieval decision and stop when the evidence is sufficient or the budget is exhausted.
articles.boundary: An agent that retrieves repeatedly can amplify an incorrect premise. More searches are not inherently better or more trustworthy.
articles.example: A comparison question retrieves specifications for both products before generating a supported contrast.
articles.application: Multi-document analysis where evidence coverage can be audited.

articles.title: Fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA and PEFT
articles.concept: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts selected trainable parameters while keeping most pretrained weights frozen. LoRA expresses weight updates through two low-rank matrices.
articles.mechanism: For a weight matrix with output and input dimensions, LoRA trains rank-sized factors whose product approximates the update. QLoRA combines quantized frozen base weights with trainable adapters; computation and optimizer precision remain separate choices. Version the tokenizer, training data, adapter configuration, and base model, and evaluate on held-out tasks and safety cases.
articles.boundary: Fine-tuning changes behavior but is not a reliable database update mechanism. Low parameter counts do not remove data quality or evaluation requirements.
articles.example: A support model is adapted to produce a consistent answer format using reviewed examples.
articles.application: Task adaptation where full fine-tuning is too expensive and behavior needs to change.

articles.title: Quantization and precision tradeoffs
articles.concept: Quantization represents numbers with a smaller set of discrete values. Scale and zero point map values between integer storage and an approximate floating-point representation.
articles.mechanism: Choose a calibration strategy and quantization granularity appropriate to the model. Quantize values within a supported range and measure reconstruction error, then evaluate end-task quality and serving performance. Distinguish weight-only methods from activation quantization and verify that the runtime actually supports the selected format efficiently.
articles.boundary: Lower bit width does not guarantee lower latency on every device. Outliers, kernels, and conversion overhead can dominate.
articles.example: A local model uses a smaller weight representation to fit memory, then compares answer quality against its baseline.
articles.application: Resource-constrained inference and memory-efficient model deployment.

articles.title: LangChain, LangGraph and durable state
articles.concept: Workflow orchestration connects model calls, retrieval, and tools. A state graph makes transitions explicit and can support checkpoints and controlled resumptions.
articles.mechanism: Define a typed state containing only information needed across steps. Nodes return explicit updates, edges encode routing, and checkpoints persist progress. Treat external side effects separately from state transitions: replaying a node must not duplicate purchases or messages. Bound retries and route ambiguous or high-impact actions to review.
articles.boundary: A checkpoint is not a guarantee that external side effects happened exactly once. Framework abstractions do not replace authorization and idempotency.
articles.example: A research workflow pauses after collecting evidence and resumes after a human approves the draft.
articles.application: Long-running assistant workflows requiring inspection, recovery, and review.

articles.title: MCP, tools, memory and multi-agent systems
articles.concept: MCP standardizes communication between AI applications and external capabilities. Tool availability does not imply that an agent is authorized to execute every exposed operation.
articles.mechanism: Separate the client, connection lifecycle, capability discovery, tool schema validation, and application authorization. Give each agent the least privilege needed, preserve provenance when agents exchange messages, and bound shared memory. Treat tool results and remote descriptions as untrusted inputs, especially when they can influence later actions.
articles.boundary: A tool schema validates shape, not business authorization or truth. Multi-agent discussion does not establish independent evidence if all agents share the same faulty source.
articles.example: A read-only research agent delegates a calculation to a restricted tool without receiving write privileges.
articles.application: Tool-connected assistants with explicit access boundaries and auditable actions.

articles.title: Building a grounded GenAI application
articles.concept: A complete application combines ingestion, retrieval, generation, user identity, and a usable evidence display. Correctness depends on the boundaries between these components.
articles.mechanism: Validate uploads, assign tenant-owned document IDs, process asynchronously, and expose ingestion status. Retrieve only active authorized revisions. Render citations through validated identifiers, escape generated text, and keep request traces free of unnecessary sensitive content. Evaluate complete user journeys, including deletion and permission changes, rather than only model responses.
articles.boundary: A successful model response does not prove that uploads, deletion, authorization, and citations work correctly across the application.
articles.example: A team knowledge assistant displays source passages and removes deleted documents from future answers.
articles.application: End-to-end document assistants with trustworthy provenance and lifecycle behavior.

questions.title: What problem does MCP solve for an AI application?
questions.answer:
It provides a common protocol for connecting applications with external capabilities. Authentication, authorization, and safe application behavior still need deliberate design.

Separate the client, connection lifecycle, capability discovery, tool schema validation, and application authorization. Give each agent the least privilege needed, preserve provenance when agents exchange messages, and bound shared memory. Treat tool results and remote descriptions as untrusted inputs, especially when they can influence later actions.

A tool schema validates shape, not business authorization or truth. Multi-agent discussion does not establish independent evidence if all agents share the same faulty source.
